paras: The threatened lynching of Lewis Hubbard took place in Ridgely, a village adjoining Springfield, Illinois, in early May 1903, when posses hunted Hubbard, a Black man accused of shooting and killing the village constable, Peter Heck. Wire reports said that if the village posses captured him he would be "summarily dealt with," but he was arrested the next day and said he had fired in self-defense.

According to Cyrus Ford, a Ridgely resident, he and Heck went on May 3 to a timbered tract next to Oak Ridge Park to arrest young men and women who had been "making themselves obnoxious" to residents nearby. The St. Louis Republic described Heck as city marshal of Ridgely, while the wire report called him a constable.

In Ford's account, a man and a woman drove up in a buggy, Heck tried to arrest the man, and in the scuffle that followed the man drew a revolver and shot him in the breast. Heck fired two shots after he was wounded, but the man and the woman escaped, leaving the buggy behind; Ford drove Heck in it to the city physician, and he died within the hour. The Republic's first dispatch did not name the gunman, but the wire report identified him as "a negro named Lewis Hubbard" and described a "desperate fight" during an attempted arrest.

The shooting set off a search for the gunman. The Republic reported "intense excitement" and "a mob" searching the neighborhood "with the avowed intention of wreaking vengeance on Heck's slayer." The wire account said the entire police and sheriff's forces were scouring the country and that Hubbard would be "summarily dealt with" if any of the village posses found him.

Hubbard was arrested on Monday, May 4, with no mob action reported. He said that Heck and four other men insulted a woman who was with him, that they assaulted him when he objected, and that he shot Heck in self-defense. No report of an inquest, indictment or trial, or of what became of Hubbard after his arrest, appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers mostly as short wire items in small-town weeklies from South Dakota to Mississippi. Its first version ran under headlines such as "Negro Murders a Constable" and "Illinois Posse is Searching for Negro Murderer," and it reported the posses' threat without comment. The St. Louis Republic's special dispatch, sent before the gunman was identified, named no race and drew on Ford's eyewitness account.

The follow-up, headed "He Claims Self-Defense" or "Murderer of Constable Arrested," gave Hubbard's version but still called him the man "who shot and killed" Heck. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

Accounts of the shooting differ, and each comes from one side. Ford said Heck was making an arrest for nuisance behavior at the park, the wire report spoke of a fight during an arrest, and Hubbard said Heck's party had insulted his companion and assaulted him first. The wire item has the shooting at "an early hour Sunday morning," while the arrest report places it on Sunday night.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Lewis Hubbard
bases: Village posses and a mob hunted Hubbard with a stated threat to deal with him summarily, but he was arrested without any reported attack [A9][A2][A5].
The St. Louis Republic special [A2] and the separate wire report [A9] independently report the shooting and the vengeful search, and the arrest is reported in a further wire item [A5].

accounts.label: Witness Ford (St. Louis Republic special)
accounts.gist: Heck went with Ford to arrest young people who frequented a timbered tract near Oak Ridge Park; when he tried to arrest a man who drove up with a woman, a scuffle followed and the man shot him in the breast and escaped with the woman.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A Black man, Lewis Hubbard, shot Heck in a 'desperate fight' as the constable tried to arrest him; village posses would deal with him summarily if they caught him.

accounts.label: Hubbard's statement after arrest
accounts.gist: Heck and four others insulted a woman who was with him; when he resented it he was assaulted, and he shot Heck in self-defense.

framing.detail: Wire headlines 'Negro Murders a Constable' and 'Illinois Posse is Searching for Negro Murderer' named race and treated the posses' threat as matter-of-fact news.
The St. Louis Republic's special named no race and reported the mob's 'avowed intention of wreaking vengeance' without comment.
The follow-up ran under 'He Claims Self-Defense' or 'Murderer of Constable Arrested', still calling Hubbard the man 'who shot and killed' Heck.

versions.value: Heck tried to arrest the man at a tract near Oak Ridge Park; the man drew a revolver in a scuffle (Ford)
Desperate fight as the constable attempted to arrest 'the negro' (wire)
Heck and four others insulted a woman with Hubbard and assaulted him; he fired in self-defense (Hubbard)

conflicts.note: Each version comes from one side: the officer's companion, an unattributed wire, or the accused.
Minor; both describe him as the village's officer.
The arrest item, written after the fact, says Sunday night; the date May 3 is consistent in both.

record_check.dossier: Black: the wire calls Hubbard 'a negro'
At large during the posse search on May 3-4, then arrested Monday, May 4
Village posses ('a mob' in the St. Louis Republic), alongside police and sheriff's forces
The one death is the officer, Peter Heck, killed by Hubbard; his race is not stated; no Black person was reported killed
Five independent-text items plus six reprints in white papers, May 4-9; nothing found in the Black press

info: Night of Sunday, May 3, 1903 (wire: 'Sunday night'/'last night'; Hot Springs text: 'an early hour Sunday morning')
Ridgely (also printed Ridgley), a village or suburb adjoining Springfield, Illinois; Ford placed the shooting at a timbered tract adjoining Oak Ridge Park
Lewis Hubbard, called 'a negro' in the wire report, was the target of the posses' threat; Peter Heck, the officer, was killed
Hubbard was accused of shooting and killing Peter Heck, constable or city marshal of Ridgely, during an attempted arrest
Posses from the village (wire) or 'a mob' (St. Louis Republic) searched for the slayer; police and sheriff's forces also searched
No report of what followed the arrest (jail, inquest, indictment, trial, or any mob attempt) appears in the coverage

News brief: Cyrus Ford of Ridgely, brother of Constable Gabe Ford, fatally wounded July 26 by John McCue; a separate shooting.
